look_here_first: LOOK FIRST underground: tough/wiry stolons and usually small (~3–8 mm) tubers distinguish purple nutsedge in combination with persistent, often purplish/red-brown ~2.6–3.4 mm scales. Don't rely on reddish seedhead color by itself.

project_inclusion.range_basis: POWO lists Cyperus rotundus as introduced in Texas; retain in learner for weed lookalike recognition only, exclude from native-only calculations.

morphology_keys.habit: Introduced perennial sedge, frequently colonial in cultivated or disturbed ground.
morphology_keys.underground: Hard, wiry stolons bearing tubers commonly 3–8 mm; compare with yellow nutsedge softer stolons and usually larger tubers.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Terminal umbel-like rays with flattened spikelets; scales often red-purple-brown but variable.
morphology_keys.scales: Persistent mature floral scales often ~2.6–3.4 mm with reddish/purple tint; ranges overlap other taxa.
morphology_keys.fruit: One-seeded achene; macro of scale and fruit needed for strong ID.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Purple versus yellow nutsedge: examine an intact underground system before deciding. C. rotundus often produces chains of smaller tubers connected by wiry rhizomes; C. esculentus more often has single terminal tubers. Both vary, so combine this with mature spikelet scales and other floral characters; reddish versus yellowish color alone is unreliable. C. strigosus is another sedge look-alike, often with different spikelet and rhizome/tuber characters; a triangular stem only confirms a sedge, not the species.
comparisons.cautions: Photo source geography is not evidence of three-county target zone native range; colors and many measurements overlap, require mature specimens.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: Start with an intact underground connection: purple nutsedge often has small dark tubers joined along tough, slender rhizomes, sometimes in chains. Above ground, check the triangular flowering stalk and flattened, often reddish-brown spikelets; color alone does not separate it from yellow nutsedge.

crew_field_sequence.field_check: Where already exposed, photograph the shoot, connecting slender rhizome, and several attached tubers in one frame with a ruler. Record whether tubers occur in chains; a single detached tuber is not enough.
Photograph the full sedge crown, then the narrow flattened spikelets. A triangular stem indicates a sedge, not which nutsedge species.
On a mature spikelet, isolate a scale with a millimeter ruler. Existing reference describes C. rotundus scales around 2.6–3.4 mm, but measurements overlap yellow nutsedge.
Use a macro or microscope with scale for the fruit and style branches. Do not infer these details from the existing spikelet photographs.

local_look_alikes.separation: Usually produces individual terminal tubers on softer rhizomes rather than multiple small tubers in chains; often straw-colored spikelets. Both characters vary, so check intact underground growth and measured mature scales together.
Also has triangular sedge culms and clustered spikelets. Do not call it purple nutsedge without showing the distinctive tuber-bearing underground system and mature floral structures.
